articles.title: They lost weight with a GLP-1. Then their spending changed in ways they never saw coming.
articles.summary: Paying for GLP-1 medications is just the beginning. The drugs can reshape how people spend and save — and even what they’re willing to splurge on.
articles.body:
As Ozempic's popularity soared in the early 2020s, its eye-popping cost — more than $1,000 for a month's supply, in some cases — made headlines . With more GLP-1 options now on the market, broader insurance coverage for the drugs to treat additional conditions and the proliferation of cheaper compounded versions, prices have slowly begun to come down, putting the medications within reach for more people.

For those self-paying for the weight loss versions of the medications, one month of Wegovy now costs between $349 and $499, depending on the dose, while Zepbound's prices now range from $299 to $449 for four weeks of doses.

Meanwhile, GLP-1 drugs are changing the way people shop and eat. They helped fuel the protein-maxxing craze , triggered what some have called a " structural disruption" to the food and beverage industry, and even changed what ends up in people's grocery carts. Within six months of starting the medications, people cut their supermarket spending by 5.3% , while savory snack purchases dropped by more than 11%.

I've been reporting on GLP-1 medications for years now and have interviewed dozens of people who have taken the medication. If there's one thing that's become clear, it's that when the medications work as hoped, they set in motion a cascade of changes in people's lives. Controlled blood sugar and weight loss are just the beginning for many people, who find their cravings for less nutritious snacks fade away, their desire to drink alcohol ebbs and their healthier habits and routines become easier to stick to.

The same goes for their personal finances: The cost of GLP-1s themselves is only the first of many budgetary changes that come with the weekly shot.

The associate dean saving thousands on takeout

When I first spoke to Michael Donnelly-Boylen in 2025, the 52-year-old had a new lease on life — literally. He'd felt so long that he was fighting a losing battle against his health issues that he was " preparing for death ," Donnelly-Boylen told me. Meanwhile, he and his husband were spending as much as $75 a day on delivery orders for lunch, dinner and sometimes breakfast. On the rare occasion that he or his husband did go grocery shopping, their haul was "almost entirely snacks," Donnelly-Boylen says. "Maybe we'd buy eggs and milk, but a lot of that was just to bake goodies; it wasn't for good use."

Then he started taking Mounjaro — and his appetite, eating habits and spending changed.

Now, Donnelly-Boylen only uses meal delivery services to order healthy, protein-rich foods to his hotel when he travels. That amounts to about $2,000 saved per month. It more than covers the "bougie" groceries he buys now (though, he does still get them via Instacart — "I don't like the carts and the people, it's just madness," Donnelly-Boylen says). The foods he stocks in his fridge aren't cheap, but they're packed with nutrients and contain far less fat and fewer ultraprocessed ingredients than what Donnelly-Boylen used to eat. "If you told me two years ago that my favorite snack would be cottage cheese with berries, I would've told you you're crazy — but that's my life these days," he says.

Donnelly-Boylen was also able to quit taking other prescriptions, including his blood pressure medication, and he's lost virtually all interest in alcohol (which he previously spent about $200 a month on). But of course there are new expenses — including an air fryer, blender and a soft serve machine to support his new healthy cooking habits.

Then there were the clothes. As Donnelly-Boylen started losing weight, his clothing size quickly went down. And each new size meant buying at least enough new clothes to look professional at work events. Eventually, though, he reached his husband's lower weight and started wearing his hand-me-downs. Donnelly-Boylen's husband had gone up in size, so he started taking a GLP-1 drug too and began losing weight. So the pair keep about half of their clothes in a storage unit. "Now I shop in the storage unit," says Donnelly-Boylen.

In total, the savings — especially on takeout — mean that Donnelly-Boylen's monthly spending is down by almost $2,000. But there's a catch. While his own GLP-1 is covered by insurance and costs him just $25 a month, his husband's medication is not, and costs $330 per month. "The savings that I got, a lot of that is being eaten by [the cost of] his medication," says Donnelly-Boylen.

The stroke survivor spending on travel and fashion

After ShantaQuilette Carter-Williams suffered a stroke in her early 40s, her doctor said her weight was putting her life at risk and recommended a GLP-1. But her insurance wouldn't cover it, so she'd have to pay $1,600 a month out of pocket. "I was like, 'I'm gonna die because I can't afford that,'" Carter-Williams told Yahoo in a previous interview . But then she found out she had type 2 diabetes, a diagnosis that many GLP-1 users have told me is both a blessing and a curse. No one wants a potentially life-threatening illness, but it did mean her insurance would cover Ozempic, with a co-pay of just $25.

Food has always been — and remains — an important way for Carter-Williams and her family to connect. But instead of DoorDashing meals, regularly eating three-course dinners out with her husband and getting snacks delivered from grocery stores, Carter-Williams now shops at Sprouts and has memberships to healthier meal delivery services, including Gardencup . The individual grocery items might be more expensive, but she estimates she still saves several hundred dollars a month on food just by eating less. Carter-Williams and her husband still treat themselves to dinner out, but she says, "My appetite is not as big, and it's more managed."

One look at Carter-Williams on social media and it's clear: She's a woman with her own style. "The girlies love the clothes; bigger or smaller, that's right," she says. But plus-size clothing brands were often expensive. After taking a GLP-1 (Carter-Williams went off hers in February of 2025, but has maintained her weight loss), she can now buy clothes from more affordable retailers. "I can shop at a lot of different stores economically that I couldn't before," allowing her to buy more items she loves without a bigger hit to her wallet.

Along with new shopping destinations, Carter-Williams's improved health has made her want to travel to new places. With her weight and key health measures under control, she was able to take fewer medications and wanted to make the most of her newfound energy. First stop: Costa Rica for zip-lining and canyoning (though, she later realized, these adrenaline-pumping activities are still high-risk for stroke survivors and those with heart conditions).

Surprisingly, traveling to new parts of the world hasn't increased her vacation spending. "When we traveled internationally, we used to get business class so you could lay down," Carter-Williams says. "But that costs a lot more, right? And I would have to do that because I couldn't fit comfortably in a [standard cabin] chair." A first-class seat on a flight to Turkey earlier this year would have cost Carter-Williams $11,000, she says. But she opted for economy. "I can literally comfortably stretch my legs out and do all those things that I didn't realize [were] an issue until they weren't an issue," she says.

The plus-size influencer who's been freed from the 'fat tax'

Andy Neal rose to internet fame for taking " stupid hikes for [his] stupid mental health. " His therapist had recommended he take up hiking to help him recover from his binge eating disorder. Neal is also a filmmaker. His footage of the gorgeous trails he was walking, paired with his mildly self-deprecating humor and totally unironic joy, caught the attention of major brands, including Nike and REI. That marked the launch of a new phase of his career as a plus-size model and influencer. But when brands weren't giving him free items, "the plus-size stores were so prohibitively expensive," Neal tells Yahoo.

Despite his active lifestyle, Neal's weight remained consistently high. Long hikes left him debilitatingly sore. By adding time in the gym and making changes to his diet, he managed to lose 40 pounds, but the scale wouldn't drop below 360 pounds. After some initial skepticism, Neal decided to try a GLP-1 medication in June 2025. Within six months, he'd lost 100 pounds.

The medication costs him $199 for a four-week supply of shots. "We definitely had to make some adjustments" in terms of finances, Neal says. He and his wife combed through their subscriptions — canceling streaming services they didn't use much and Neal's $60-per-month LinkedIn Premium subscription, which served its purpose maybe once a year — to make room in their budget for his tirzepatide. The cost has since gone up for his dose, but "it's fine — the way it's changed my life, I don't mind paying for it," Neal says.

He estimates that the medication has slashed his personal food spending by about half. But, with a growing 13-year-old daughter who's into basketball, the family's overall meal budget is about the same — it just consists of a lot more healthy groceries and far fewer snacks or takeout meals. And they still pay for their $110 monthly gym membership, "but I'm using it much more consistently," says Neal. "I used to say it was a monthly fat tax."

As for his wardrobe spending? Like Carter-Williams, Neal is spending less per item, but he hasn't exactly saved money. "My wife gets onto me because, before, I couldn't go into a store and buy whatever I wanted, so I'm trying things stylewise that I couldn't before," Neal says. As a result, he's spending several hundred dollars a month on clothes, including suits and dress clothes that he needs to wear to influencer conferences.

In total, his monthly spending has increased slightly — by about $70 — since starting a GLP-1. "I do it gladly …I know it's privileged, but these are costs that, when you talk to your doctor, nobody talks to you about," says Neal.

The cookbook author investing in her health — without giving up the things she loves

Suzy Chase lives in New York City — which, in her words, means that life is expensive any way you slice it. But she's always paid for her beloved workout classes because they are "my social time, my therapy, my everything, all wrapped into one," Chase previously told Yahoo. The one thing they didn't do for her, however, was help her lose weight. And when menopause and the COVID-19 pandemic hit at the same time, Chase's weight crept up.

Then she learned about the GLP-1, Zepbound. The weekly injections helped Chase lose 50 pounds and set the 59-year-old's sights on a new goal: "training for 80." She didn't qualify for insurance coverage, so Chase was at first paying $1,080 per month out of pocket for her medication. Yet even with the added cost of the medication, Chase says being on a GLP-1 hasn't otherwise changed how she spends her money or time. She still goes to the same two workout studios and pays the same amount for the classes, "but now I'm seeing my hard work paying off," she says.

As a cookbook author and podcaster , Chase has never scrimped on groceries, and she still doesn't. But her shopping and eating habits have changed. Instead of roaming the center aisles of the grocery store where the snacks live, "I am definitely shopping the perimeter of the grocery store a lot more," Chase says. "I'm not saving money, [I've] just pivoted from a lot of red meat to vegetarian and pescatarian foods." The biggest adjustment to her budget was replacing her wardrobe — at a cost of about $3,500 in total — as her size changed. "I've had to get everything new, but it's been slowly over time," she says.

Chase eventually switched to getting her Zepbound from Lilly Direct, where her 2.5-milligram dose costs $299 per month. And she's figured out a way to maintain her weight and her account balance: Chase now spaces her doses out every 15 days (instead of every seven), bringing her prorated monthly cost down to about $150, she estimates. "Tweaking my dose has been really good for the budget," she says. "I sort of changed my mindset, and now I think about [Zepbound] as a support tool and not the solution. Spacing my doses and retraining how I think about food has made a world of difference."

The teacher paying for her GLP-1 with takeout savings

After caring for her grandmother in the final days of her life as she suffered from complications of rheumatoid arthritis, Cassandra Smith knew she didn't want to face the same fate. Smith had been diagnosed with the autoimmune disease by age 30 and was already dealing with debilitating flare-ups. Her doctor told her that inflammation from being overweight was only making it worse. Starting a Mediterranean diet helped, but it didn't get Smith anywhere near a healthy BMI.

She knew that a GLP-1 drug would help her lose weight , which would, in turn, help with the symptoms of her autoimmune condition. But the medications aren't approved to treat rheumatoid arthritis, so her insurance wouldn't cover them. Smith instead gets her compounded tirzepatide from a telehealth company and pays $399 a month for it. That's no small sum, but Smith told herself, "You're not eating out, you're cooking at home and you're going to pay for your medicine," she tells Yahoo. "I basically took the money [for the GLP-1] out of my eating-out habit."

Smith cut what she spent dining out with her daughter from about $200 a month to about $50. When the pair goes to their favorite Chinese restaurant, they each order a $5 kids' meal. "The lady there is even like, 'Oh, ya'll want the kids' meal?' She knows the drill," Smith says.

Her grocery bill has also shrunk, from $550 a month to $320. "My bill has definitely gone down because I don't get all the snacks, I don't get all the different cereals, or all the flour, oil — all the extra stuff you have to do to basically eat unhealthy," she says. Smith's preferred proteins are fish and red meat, which can be pricey. But otherwise, she tries to eat raw fruits and vegetables most of the time. "I don't buy as many ingredients anymore," she says. "The ingredients I am buying are still a little expensive, but I don't have to add anything additional to them."

Some of Smith's expenses have increased, though. Before taking a GLP-1 drug, she didn't have a workout routine. Now Smith goes to Pilates at least once a week and has joined a gym. She also bought a membership to a "jump house" for kids — where she sometimes jumps alongside her daughter.

Like exercise, fashion was a $0 line item in Smith's monthly budget because she "hated" clothes before starting a GLP-1 medication. But losing weight has led to investing in a new, colorful wardrobe to match her church choir's weekly themes.

On the whole, Smith says she's still saving several hundred dollars a month. "If I say I'm not going to do something, I'm not going to do it," she says. And for the moments when she's tempted to let her resolve soften, Smith has "a little 5-year-old accountability partner" in her daughter. "It's kind of hard to do the wrong thing when she's always with me."

articles.title: Walmart sees sales growth slip as US shoppers feel the squeeze
articles.summary: High gas prices and weaker pharmacy sales pushed Walmart's growth to its slowest pace in six years
articles.body:
Sales at the US retail giant Walmart grew at their slowest pace for more than six years in the most recent quarter, suggesting American shoppers are under strain.

Walmart, which due to its size is well-placed to gauge consumers' mood, blamed the rising price of fuel.

Sales at comparable sites across the chain were up by 2.6%, excluding fuel, between May and July the company said.

Walmart said it would use up to $3bn of expected tariff refunds to lower prices in a bid to keep customers spending.

The rebate stems from duties the retailer paid after President Trump imposed a wave of tariffs on imported goods last year. Retailers are receiving refunds from central government after those tariffs were ruled unlawful.

Rival retailer Target recently said it had received $1bn in rebates, boosting its profits.

Walmart, the US's largest retailer, said the nearly $3bn in tariff rebate it anticipated would help it continue a programme of price cuts or "rollbacks" that it expanded earlier this year .

Walmart has leaned heavily on price cuts to retain customers, launching 11,000 of its so-called "rollbacks" across categories.

Chief financial officer John David Rainey said those lower prices were already lifting transactions and unit sales, especially in food and other staples like toys.

But he acknowledged that the retail environment remained uneven, with lower-income households – a core part of Walmart's base – feeling squeezed.

Rainey said rising petrol prices were leaving shoppers with less spare cash, saying the shift in behaviour became clear once fuel went above $4 a gallon.

Price moves in June made the impact obvious, he added, with lower-income customers pulling back and focusing spending on essentials.

Beyond the consumer pullback, Walmart's results highlighted several additional risks that could shape the firm's prospects in the months ahead.

Much of the quarter's profit lift came from tariff refunds that had already come in, a one-off benefit that analysts say won't recur to the same extent.

The price rollbacks could put pressure on margins, while Walmart is also spending money on automation, new warehouses, and tech upgrades.

On the earnings call, analysts pressed management on whether lower prices were already driving a lift in sales and whether some rollbacks could be locked in for 2027.

Walmart said the benefits were showing up most clearly in food and other staples, and that certain cuts might remain if they continued to resonate with shoppers.

"Our hope and intention always is that rollbacks can become permanent ... wherever possible," Rainey said.

Analysts also questioned whether Walmart's income could continue to grow despite flagging sales. Executives said they believed it could, pointing to businesses such as membership and advertising.

articles.title: Arctic power play gives top US adversary new opening with Russia as US stakes grow
articles.summary: China launched seasonal container service to Europe via Russia's Arctic Northern Sea Route, raising U.S. concerns over the Polar Silk Road strategy.
articles.body: China is testing whether the top of the world can become a new strategic trade corridor, launching regular seasonal container service to Europe through Russia’s Arctic as Beijing and Moscow deepen their commercial and military footprint in a region Washington increasingly views as critical to U.S. security. The service remains limited in scale, with just over eight voyages planned this season, but China analyst Gordon Chang told Fox News Digital that its significance goes beyond the number of containers currently making the journey. "China has a major strategic push on the Arctic for various reasons," Chang said in an interview. "Arctic ice is melting, and this means that the Northern Sea Route, which hugs Russia's north coast, does become viable at least for a few months in the summer." TRUMP ENVOY WARNS CHINA'S POWER MOVE AT SEA IS THREAT 'WE CANNOT AFFORD TO IGNORE' Sea Legend Shipping’s Dubai Tower departed Ningbo-Zhoushan Port on Aug. 15 for Europe via Russia’s Northern Sea Route, with the journey to Felixstowe, England, scheduled to take about 20 days, according to China Daily on Aug. 17. The move comes as a new U.S. congressional commission staff report warns that Russia’s increasing isolation and dependence on Beijing are giving China greater leverage — including greater access to the Arctic. Chang warned that Washington needs a stronger physical presence in response. "We need to be in the Arctic, and President Trump has authorized more icebreakers," he told Fox News Digital. "We are woefully short in that department." TIM SHEEHY EXPOSES A 'SCARY' SHIPBUILDING COLLAPSE THAT LEAVES THE US VULNERABLE TO CHINA A White House official told Fox News Digital on background that, "The Arctic is a critical region for U.S. national security and the economy. As an Arctic nation, the United States will pursue its security and economic interests and ensure safety, stability, and prosperity in the face of growing competition from China and Russia." A fact sheet released Aug. 20 by staff of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and subsequent economic isolation from the West have "compelled Russia to accept a greater Chinese presence in the Arctic," a region Moscow has traditionally regarded as central to its sovereignty and national security. CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE The report said Chinese state-owned enterprises now hold a combined 20% stake in the U.S.- and EU-sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project, while China and Russia are developing year-round commercial shipping along the Northern Sea Route. The two countries have also established a joint venture to manufacture ice-class container vessels, with the first ship planned to enter service in 2027. The Pentagon’s 2024 Arctic Strategy similarly said changing climate conditions are increasing accessibility in the region while China seeks greater influence and access there. The strategy identified Beijing’s proposed "Polar Silk Road" as a vehicle for infrastructure and natural-resource investments in the Arctic and warned that growing cooperation between China and Russia could "‘alter the Arctic’s stability and threat picture.’" For China-Europe commerce, the Northern Sea Route offers a radically different path from the traditional westbound journey through the Strait of Malacca, Indian Ocean, Bab el-Mandeb, Red Sea and Suez Canal. "This of course avoids some choke points, like the Strait of Malacca, the Bab el-Mandeb, the Suez Canal, the Strait of Gibraltar," Chang said. "So this is important for China." The new USCC report argues that China is increasingly benefiting from an asymmetric relationship in which Moscow needs Beijing more than Beijing needs Moscow. It says China has become indispensable to Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, giving Beijing growing leverage to obtain discounted energy and greater access to Russian military technology while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance. Energy is a major part of that imbalance. According to the report, China accounts for roughly half of Russia’s crude oil exports, while Russian crude represents only about one-fifth of China’s oil imports. The report says China has purchased approximately $372 billion in Russian fossil fuels since the invasion of Ukraine. UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC Moscow is now making increasingly aggressive use of the same Arctic passage to move oil east. Reuters reported Aug. 11 that Russia had sent seven crude shipments totaling roughly 6 million barrels toward Asia through the Northern Sea Route so far this season, nearly half the amount transported during the entire 2025 season. China is the principal destination for those shipments, according to Reuters. The growing Arctic activity comes as Washington has become increasingly concerned about Chinese and Russian cooperation close to Alaska. Chang pointed to the Bering Strait — separating Russia from Alaska — as a strategic vulnerability even on the Arctic route. CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS "There is one choke point though, which is of interest," he said. "You have to go between Russia on the west and our 49th state on the east. And that gives the U.S. some leverage over here." The military relationship is also expanding. The new USCC fact sheet says China and Russia had participated in at least 119 combined military exercises as of April 2026, while their joint naval operations in July included submarine, anti-submarine and drone activity. It also noted that Chinese bombers entered the Alaskan Air Defense Identification Zone for the first time during a joint China-Russia bomber patrol in 2024. For Chang, the issue extends beyond whether the Northern Sea Route itself ever becomes a competitor to Suez. "There are some U.S. national security strategists who say, ‘Oh, the Arctic is a distraction. There are more important places in the world,’" Chang said. "So we've got no choice to respond. Whether we think the Arctic is strategic or not, the Chinese and Russians are there in force. We have to be there too." articles.title: UK, France, Germany, Italy and Canada condemn Israel's West Bank settlement project
articles.summary: European countries and Canada pile on pressure over Israel's plans to expand settlements in a strategically vital part of the occupied West Bank.
articles.body:
Israel's plans to open up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank have sparked fresh condemnation by major Western powers.

In a joint statement, the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Canada called the decision "unacceptable" , external and urged Israel to "retract the plans immediately".

All settlements are illegal under international law and, under international pressure, Israel held off for decades on plans to build in E1 to the east of Jerusalem.

Many of its allies and Palestinians argued this development would deal a major blow to hopes of a two-state solution, effectively cutting the West Bank in two and isolating east Jerusalem .

BBC speaks to Palestinians targeted by Israeli settlers

"At a time of grave instability in the West Bank with unprecedented levels of violence by settlers against civilians, and serious restrictions on the Palestinian economy, this decision is even more concerning," the statement from the European allies and Canada published on Thursday said.

"Not only will they [the plans] take us further from peace, but they further undermine Israel's international standing," the statement added.

In a separate statement, the UN secretary general also said the E1 plan posed an "existential threat" to a contiguous Palestinian state - and so did Belgium's foreign minister.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's condemnation earlier on Thursday had drawn "outright" rejection by the Israeli foreign minister.

Despite an Israeli court challenge to the plans by Bedouin Palestinians living in the area and Israeli peace groups, on Wednesday the Israeli housing ministry issued a tender for 1,234 of the 3,401 housing units approved by the Israeli government last August .

It covers about 12 sq km (4.6 sq miles) between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Maale Adumim.

At the time of their unveiling, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich - an ultranationalist and settler - said the idea of a Palestinian state was "being erased".

The deadline for bids is 19 October, just days before Israel's general election on 27 October , making it much harder for any future government to overturn any tenders issued.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

Despite the fierce international opposition, successive Israeli governments have allowed settlements to grow.

However, expansion has risen sharply since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returned to power in late 2022 at the head of a right-wing, pro-settler coalition, as well as the start of the Gaza war, triggered by Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

Opponents of the E1 project have warned that it would effectively block the establishment of a Palestinian state because it would cut off the north of the West Bank from the south, and prevent the development in the centre of a contiguous Palestinian urban area connecting Ramallah, East Jerusalem and Bethlehem.

articles.title: Trump administration announces new sanctions on Cuba, escalating economic pressure
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new sanctions Thursday against Cuban individuals and entities, part of the Trump administration’s escalating pressure campaign against the communist regime in Havana. The latest sanctions target leaders of the Cuban Institute of Friendship with the Peoples (ICAP), which Rubio said exploits educational exchange with the goal of “identifying, cultivating,…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new sanctions Thursday against Cuban individuals and entities, part of the Trump administration’s escalating pressure campaign against the communist regime in Havana.

The latest sanctions target leaders of the Cuban Institute of Friendship with the Peoples (ICAP), which Rubio said exploits educational exchange with the goal of “identifying, cultivating, and radicalizing subversives.”

“The Trump Administration will not stand by while a hostile foreign power seeks to exploit our freedoms – none of which are afforded to its people – by misleading and corrupting American citizens with lies, spy tradecraft, and other malfeasance as part of the regime’s raison d’être of exporting Marxism, racial resentment, and Communist violence across the world,” Rubio said in a statement.

The administration sanctioned ICAP in June, and the actions this week blacklist the organization’s President Fernando González Llort, First Vice President Noemi Ramona Rabaza Fernandez, and North America Director Leima Martinez Freire.

The sanctions followed an event last week hosted at a cafe in Washington, D.C., that included Cuban Ambassador to the U.S. Lianys Torres Rivera, reflecting on the legacy of Fidel Castro, the repressive authoritarian leader who established the communist government.

“Just days ago, the regime attempted to use Communist kingpin and despot Fidel Castro’s 100th birthday to reinvigorate this subversive network, ferrying a new brigade of international sympathizers to Havana to network with regime officials,” Rubio said.

Other sanctions announced Thursday include four entities involved in the metals and mining industry for being state-owned or affiliated with the Cuban regime as well as three entities involved in import-export operations, including vehicles, industrial equipment, appliances and construction materials.

The U.S. also imposed sanctions on Cuba’s Ministry of Construction and a Cuban government entity supplying Cuban labor to foreign entities operating in the country.

Rubio said the new sanctions target entities “that sustain the regime’s repressive apparatus through control of key economic sectors.”

“Today’s designations make clear that the Trump Administration will not tolerate the Cuban regime’s efforts to fund its repression or continue its decades-long campaign of subversive anti-American activities,” he said.

President Trump has made trying to overthrow Cuba’s ruling communist party a priority, saying in May that the U.S. will “take over” the Caribbean nation, imposing a de facto oil blockade against the country and designating it a state sponsor of terrorism. The U.S. economic pressure campaign has led to a deepening humanitarian crisis on the island, but the country’s communist leaders have so far rejected U.S. appeals to step aside.

articles.title: Syria’s civil society navigates post-Assad era: Partnership or control?
articles.summary: Syria’s civil society grapples with redefining its role as the state reasserts itself after Assad’s fall.
articles.body:
Damascus, Syria – For most of the war , Bahjat Hajjar worked outside the Syrian state. A co-founder of the Local Administration Councils Unit, he spent years between Turkiye and opposition-held northern Syria, supporting councils that ran bakeries, clinics and schools where no government existed.

Today he sits inside the state, as deputy minister of social affairs and labour – the ministry that licenses Syria’s associations. “The relationship with civil society is one of the most important joints in the reshaping of the state itself,” he told Al Jazeera.

More than a year and a half after the fall of President Bashar al-Assad on December 8, 2024, that relationship is still unsettled. Under the old system, Hajjar said regulation of civil society was effectively run by the intelligence service: “There was no minister who passed through this ministry without security intervention or approval.” Perhaps ten associations were licensed a year, sometimes fewer.

After al-Assad’s fall – the culmination of the 13-year war – organisations that had operated from previously opposition-controlled areas and neighbouring countries were told to register in Damascus, and their numbers have risen steeply. Founding an association is now sometimes easier than founding a company, Hajjar said: procedures are simple, costs are close to nothing and the main remaining condition is that founders have no criminal convictions.

“But we should not fall into the idea that opening the door to registration automatically means we have a strong civil society,” he said. “In countries that pass through transitions, civil society does expand and multiply. The more important question is what role it will actually play.”

Syria’s civil society sector has spent 14 years trying to answer that question.

“Its development was tied to the development of events in Syria,” said Mutasem Syoufi, executive director of The Day After, which works on democratic transition. He describes a landscape assembled in layers: old charities that continued operating, new ones tied to political actors in government-held areas, relief associations born inside the uprising, rights and development organisations and the coordination committees that were established in 2011 at the beginning of the protest movement .

What organisations gained, Syoufi said, was the ability to work under pressure, a degree of institutionalisation that came with international funding and the entry of large numbers of Syrians into the sector. What they could not build was a mature civic space.

“You cannot speak of a developed civil society under conditions of war, with no stable state,” Syoufi said.

That capacity for civil society to respond to crises was built to fill a vacuum that is now closing. Yet none of the organisations interviewed said they had been pushed out by the new authorities.

Registration is open and the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour drew up its 2026–2028 strategy with civil society in the room. The unease is about direction rather than incident: limits that sound reasonable when a minister sets them out can prove more complicated on the ground, activist Alia Shams said.

The return of the state creates a fundamental dilemma for organisations that once substituted for it. The functions many took on – clinics, schools, water and shelter – are the ones ministries are now reclaiming, and the sector has to argue for a role it could previously assume was its to do in the state’s absence.

“There is still a great need for these roles, because state institutions are still weak,” said Bashar Moubarak, a civil society activist and consultant on local governance. Even with the government’s progress in working towards the rehabilitation of public hospitals and other facilities, he argues, the state cannot dispense with organisations that spent a decade in those sectors.

A crisis of local legitimacy presents a separate challenge.

Not every organisation can make the case for a continued role convincingly, because not all have standing in their own communities. Legitimacy comes from representing a community, from being trusted to close a real gap and from responding to needs identified locally rather than priorities set by donors, Moubarak said.

Organisations shaped by donor agendas rather than local ones can end up “strangers in the eyes of their own communities”.

Legal uncertainty further complicates the sector’s future. Associations are still governed by a 1958 law that requires associations to obtain prior approval for foreign funding. When a ministerial circular last October instructed them to comply with the requirement, 31 organisations signed a joint paper calling it a return to a repressive framework and urging that a new law be drafted with them. That remains under discussion.

In May, the interior ministry issued Syria’s first framework recognising peaceful assembly as a right, but requiring permission from local authorities. Rights groups have criticised those rules as too restrictive.

Civil society is also divided over how to engage with the new authorities. Shams, who has worked with various civil society organisations since 2011, divides organisations into three groups: those that have registered and are working within the new rules; those that refuse to register because they distrust the new authorities; and those that, as she puts it, “beat the drum” for the government, in that they fully back its decisions.

The space for different views has narrowed gradually since the near-total freedom of the first weeks of the post-Assad era, Shams argued. “The boundaries of civic work are being drawn right now,” Shams said, making it more urgent to defend that space today than it may be a year from now.

Organisations also face significant gaps in capacity and coordination – but not always in the obvious direction. Activists who worked underground in government-held areas had fewer opportunities to build organisational skills than colleagues in the northwest and northeast, who operated more openly and at greater scale. But they have another advantage: years of navigating the old bureaucracy have made them better at getting things through ministries. Northern organisations, Shams said, are more likely to treat paperwork as an obstruction, losing time in Damascus as a result.

Polarisation inside civil society mirrors wider society, Syoufi said. Organisations became politicised during the conflict, some documenting the victims of one side but not the other. Years of separation also left Syrians unfamiliar with one another’s experiences, while priorities diverged from region to region.

Since December 2024, he argued, a new fault line has opened between organisations aligned with the new authorities and those opposed.

“This was expected,” Syoufi said. “But civil society as a whole is still far from an agreed agenda and building one will take time.”

Moubarak, on the other hand, sees the sector as one of the few channels capable of cutting across sectarian, religious and tribal loyalties – a role tested across 14 years of war. “But if it is left alone and isolated from support, that positive role will shrink,” he said, warning that civil society could become part of the challenge rather than part of the solution.

The pull towards relief work is inherited. The law that governed associations before 2011 framed civil society as charitable and humanitarian work, Hajjar said, not as a space for public participation or influence over policy – and that law is still on the books. A decade of emergency funding reinforced the model, producing organisations well staffed to deliver services but thinly resourced for anything else. Service provision is also the least contentious role a government can ask them to perform: few object to a clinic, whereas election monitoring or documenting abuses can land an organisation in trouble.

Inside the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour, Deputy Minister Hajjar is trying to build a new relationship between the state and civil society organisations – one that, he argues, Syria has never had. It is neither the pre-2011 arrangement, when the associations’ file sat with intelligence services and no decision moved without security clearance, nor the war-years model, when organisations ran schools, clinics and rescue teams precisely because no state was there to do it.

“We do not want to return to the model of the past, where the state saw civil society as something to be controlled,” he said. “And civil society cannot be a permanent substitute for the state. What is required is neither tutelage nor conflict, but partnership.”

“During the war, when institutions were absent, civil society appeared and took on many roles,” Hajjar said. “Today, with the institutions returning, that experience should not be cancelled. It should be turned into energy that builds the new Syria.”

Syrian activist Alia Shams says that civil society organisations in the new Syria can be divided between those which have agreed to register, and those which have not, as well as others which will support the government no matter what [Ahmad Khalil Khanji/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Pollution behind coracle fishing in Carmarthenshire river's decline
articles.summary: The tradition on a Carmarthenshire river once fished by US President Jimmy Carter could be coming to an end.
articles.body:
It is a centuries-old tradition in Wales, but coracle fishers on a major river have said pollution has meant there are "no fish" left.

Testing by campaign group Save the River Tywi showed evidence of industrial, agricultural and human waste pollution, with fishers saying they often see dead fish bobbing up and down in the water.

One fifth-generation coracle fisherman described the situation in Carmarthenshire as "dire" after only catching one fish in the three-month season between May and July.

Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it took all reports of pollution seriously and had "a number of ongoing enforcement and compliance investigations within the Tywi catchment".

The tradition of coracle fishing has been part of life on the Tywi for centuries.

Typically done at night, fishermen use small rounded boats with nets cast among them to catch salmon and sewin [sea trout].

It was once an important livelihood in west Wales, but today it is mostly a heritage tradition, rather than a full-time source of income.

US President Jimmy Carter even loved fishing in these rivers , but according to fishermen, recent pollution has made it impossible.

Chairman of Carmarthen Coracle and Netsman Association, Andrew Davies, said he thought the four coracle men on the Tywi had caught 12 fish among them in the whole of the 2026 season when, a few years ago, "you'd catch that many in a night".

Keith Elias's family have been fishing on the river for 300 years - he said he had only caught one fish this season.

"It's been in my family for so long, I love carrying the tradition on, but it's getting to the point where you get to the end of the season and you're not hitting fish.

Last year, the nearby River Teifi had been noted as one of the UK's most polluted rivers , with 2,232 spills lasting more than 22,000 hours recorded in 2024.

It has been reported that some incidents of pollution were made by Welsh Water .

The company said it would invest £889m on storm overflows between 2025 and 2030, including six projects to reduce their impact on the Tywi.

It added: "We are determined to play our part to improve river water quality on the Tywi, but this isn't just an issue for water companies, collaboration is needed across sectors, including industry and agriculture, to ensure improvements."

Local people have also shared videos online of discharge across the river, which they claim appear to be from a nearby electronics recycling company Mekatek.

The company has a discharge licence from NRW.

Mekatek said it shared concerns about the drop in sewin and had spent more than "40 years developing and improving our processes to ensure we are not a factor in that reduction".

It added: "Anyone wishing to understand what we do and how well we do it is more than welcome to arrange to visit the site and view our operations for themselves."

Davies, 63, said this year's season had been "a write-off"

"I've been fishing for 38 years, I've never seen a season as bad as this," he said.

"When I first started, this river was black with fish, it was alive with fish. But it's gone now - there's no life in the river."

He said only four fishing licences had been taken out this year, compared with 12 when he started: "People have just, I won't say given up, but the enthusiasm's gone."

He said that the bad smell coming from the river "doesn't help" and he and others had reported cases of pollution to NRW "all the time", but "nothing seems to be done".

"I think something needs to be done to clean the rivers up in Wales, people have been dodging the bullet," he said.

Citizen scientists on behalf of Save the River Tywi, who have been conducting tests on the river, said there had been evidence of pollution coming from farms, companies based along the river and people.

Mayor of Carmarthen Russell Sparks said the river had been in a "really tough situation".

He added: "Over the last couple of years it's been really sad to see it, feel it and smell it."

Sparks said the smell was a combination of pollutants and algae blooms "creating this negative cycle".

In July the annual Tywi River Festival had to be cancelled because of the pollution, which Sparks said left people "absolutely devastated".

The mayor of Carmarthen automatically takes up the ancient role of Admiral of the Port and Sparks said it "breaks his heart" that his time in the role may see the end of coracle fishing.

With fishermen only catching "six sewin last year, there's a strong possibility that they won't take up their licenses next year".

Carmarthenshire MP Ann Davies wants "firmer action taken" against those who "constantly pollute the river".

She also said - as someone who farms herself - farmers have a responsibility to not pollute the river, along with people and businesses.

"We have a collective responsibility on what we buy, what we flush down the toilet."

Huwel Manley, head of south-west operations for NRW, said "Like many rivers, the Tywi faces a range of environmental pressures, including pollution and is also impacted by the current dry weather conditions which are seeing an increase in the water temperature along with wider ecological challenges.

"We take all reports of suspected pollution seriously. We currently have a number of ongoing enforcement and compliance investigations within the Tywi catchment, including cases that are progressing towards court proceedings."

The Welsh government said: "The Tywi is one of Wales' most important rivers, supporting internationally important habitats and species, local communities, recreation and cultural traditions such as coracle fishing."

It had been "aware of recent concerns regarding foam, odours and discolouration in the River Tywi" and "NRW have investigated and confirmed the impacts were linked to natural environmental conditions".

It said NRW had been investigating a separate potential source of pollution entering the Tywi and as those investigations remain ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further.

articles.title: Chanty Beluga is internet famous. Just maybe not on your internet.
articles.summary: Chanty Beluga isn't real, but her internet fame is. Meet the comedian behind the character and the strangely niche viral phenomenon she created.
articles.body:
Depending on which corner of the internet you live in, Chanty Beluga is either one of the most important women of our time or … a name that means absolutely nothing to you.

If you fall into the latter camp, here's roughly everything you need to know: Chanty Beluga is a blond, bubbly young woman who has recently begun popping up across social media, introducing herself to Uber drivers , ordering coffee and otherwise going about her fairly ordinary life. She is relentlessly cheerful and seems to be navigating the world with the confidence of someone who never once wondered whether people might find the name Chanty Beluga strange.

There's just one catch: Chanty Beluga is not a real person.

She is the creation of comedian, actor and writer Courtney O'Donnell , who came up with the name while messing around with friends on a late-night movie set. "I just was like, 'Hi, I'm Chanty,'" O'Donnell tells Yahoo. Everyone laughed. Then she added the Beluga, and everyone laughed harder. Soon, she was imagining the mundane life of a woman cursed — or blessed — with this extremely unique name.

"There's nothing to explain. She's just Chanty," says O'Donnell. And somehow, that really has been enough. "It's surprising how big it's gotten. It genuinely started as something that I found really fun. So I was like, I'll just keep doing it."

"It's a little bit of a satire of the kind of content we see now. If you're a creator and one thing pops off, you kind of have to keep doing that. So it's like, 'Part 77 of your annoying coworker,' or whatever it is," says O'Donnell. "I've certainly felt that as a person who creates on the internet."

Nearly eight years into creating comedy content online, she's taking that formula to an absurdly simple place. Instead of an elaborate premise, she is "literally a woman doing the most basic things" — but with an outlandish name.

The more interesting part of Chanty's rise, however, might be how people found her in the first place.

This wasn't a familiar story of one TikTok suddenly reaching millions of people. Chanty began on Instagram . Then she started circulating on X . O'Donnell eventually decided she should probably create a TikTok account for the character, which is where she's found her biggest audience. (Chanty has just over 83,000 followers as I'm writing this.)

In certain pockets of social media, she already has the trappings of a minor celebrity. There are fan accounts and running jokes. TikTok users have even begun inventing stories about their supposed personal encounters with her. "It's either like, 'Chanty's the nicest person ever. We went to high school together,' or like, 'She's a bitch. This is what she did,'" says O'Donnell. "One of them was that I was at Walmart and I stole Pringles and a gallon of milk out of someone's cart."

O'Donnell is happy to play along. "I think it's fun for it to be collaborative as well," she says.

Outside of those pockets, though, plenty of people have never heard of Chanty. Even some people swept up in the buzz were confused to find that her earliest videos didn't have millions of views.

"I thought she was a viral sensation," one X user posted , seemingly disappointed that Chanty's original video only had 7,854 likes when she saw it. "Bravely coming forward to say [I] don't understand why this is popping off," another poster admitted. Others disagreed : "Deserves to be seen more widely."

That disconnect gets at something both strange and interesting about internet culture now. Two people can use the same social platforms every day and come away with almost entirely different senses of what or who is popular.

"We're in this time period where sometimes we're all seeing the same thing. Sometimes we're not," says O'Donnell.

And besides: Going mainstream just isn't Chanty's style. O'Donnell says the randomness feeds into the character's lore.

"I'm glad it didn't just go to a million people at first," she says. "The nicheness of it is something that is special, and hopefully that flavor still stays."

For O'Donnell, Chanty is just another turn in a much longer attempt to figure out what kind of comedy she wants to make online. She's had other characters take off, only to find herself creatively ready to move on after eight or nine installments. The challenge, she says, has been finding the overlap between what fulfills her creatively and what people online actually want to watch.

Even though she started as an inside joke, Chanty, at least for now, has landed there. "I'm really glad that I found a place where I can create from joy," says O'Donnell.

In the meantime, she's continuing her other work, including a solo comedy show she has performed for two years. She doesn't intend for Chanty to become her entire identity. ("Imagine, I, like, change my name," she jokes.) Instead, she's treating Chanty as a project that she plans to follow only as far as it will take her.

"The second that it feels done, then it's done," says O'Donnell. "Hopefully, people have been introduced to me enough that they want to keep following along."

articles.title: Margaret Qualley wore 'barefoot sandals' on the red carpet. Are these even shoes?
articles.summary: Chanel's viral "non-shoes" have officially hit the red carpet — with Margaret Qualley's actual feet hitting it, too.
articles.body:
It's been a rocky few months for Margaret Qualley, but she put her best — and basically bare — foot forward at The Dog Stars premiere.

The actor turned heads at the premiere of the Ridley Scott film in London on Thursday, arriving in a fringed black Chanel dress and a pair of the fashion house's much-discussed "barefoot sandals."

Calling them sandals may be generous. The unusual design consists of a leather heel cap secured around the ankle, leaving the rest of Qualley's foot — including her soles and toes — completely exposed to the raw, red carpet elements.

"Calling it a shoe is too much," wrote one X user.

"OK, but the Margaret Qualley barefoot shoes are kinda horrible?" read another X comment .

There's already a dupe — one creator turned black face masks into her own toe-baring sandals.

The shoes debuted as part of Matthieu Blazy's Chanel Resort 2027 collection in April and immediately sparked strong opinions. (Not many were flattering.) The New York Times described the concept as " irrational, nonsensical luxury ," while Vogue called the unconventional footwear "freaky."

Now Qualley, a Chanel ambassador, appears to be the first celebrity brave enough to take the so-called "non-shoe" from the runway to the red carpet. She completed the look with diamond earrings, loose waves and a dark manicure and, yes, a pedicure. That's particularly important when one's toes are essentially the main accessory.

The premiere marked one of Qualley's most prominent public appearances since news broke in July that she and husband Jack Antonoff had separated after nearly three years of marriage . At the time, a representative for the actor pushed back on speculation surrounding the breakup, saying there were "no trust issues" and "no infidelity."

If Qualley was hoping to divert attention from her ring finger, the toe-baring look certainly gave everyone somewhere else to look.

The Dog Stars is a post-apocalyptic thriller that also stars Jacob Elordi as a young pilot who ventures beyond his isolated homestead after receiving a mysterious radio transmission. It's in theaters on Friday, Aug. 28.

articles.title: French becoming more effective in stopping small boat crossings, UK says
articles.summary: The Home Office credits France with intercepting hundreds of potential crossings this summer using new tactics.
articles.body:
French police tactics are becoming more effective in stopping small boats in the English Channel from reaching Britain, the Home Office has said.

It credits French authorities with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants this summer over four separate weeks, as well as stopping 12 boats at sea using new techniques.

Footage released by French police shows officers racing across a beach in jeeps to intercept a launch. Once the boat is abandoned, an officer slashes it lengthways with a knife.

The Conservatives described the announcement as a "joke" and said Channel crossing preventions were "down by half over the past year".

Migrants can be seen throwing objects at the officers, one of whom appears to respond with pepper spray.

While Channel crossings are down about 40% compared to last year, thousands of illegal migrants are getting through with 250 arriving on Monday.

In late July a record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat with Border Security Command pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on 23 July.

The Home Office, citing French police figures, said that since it struck a deal with France three months ago which included additional funding for authorities, 61% of small boats have been intercepted - a five per cent increase compared to last year.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the "UK-France deal is already having a real impact".

The UK-France Border Security deal agreed in April under the Starmer government, includes Â£501m over three years to strengthen operations in northern France and Â£161m for new approaches.

Previously the French authorities allowed most dinghies to head towards the UK once they had launched, because of the risk of intercepting them in deep water, while loaded with people.

Of the 12 dinghies stopped so far at sea, three interceptions took place in the last two weeks.

The techniques being used have not been disclosed by the UK or France.

Charlie Eastaugh, director of maritime and small boats at the Border Security Command, told the BBC that "last Thursday alone, the French prevented all three of the boats that tried to cross".

Speaking to the BBC at the Western Jetfoil facility in Dover used to process migrants, he said: "Two of those they prevented at sea, and one they prevented on land."

Between 1 January and 24 August 2026, a total of 15,897 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 44% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 42% of asylum applications between April 2025 to March 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 25 August 2025 to 24 August 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to âsmash the gangsâ behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from April 2025 to March 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,000 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,535 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from April 2025 to March 2026. This was down by 22% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

He said some had claimed bad weather was the biggest factor in a reduction of crossings this year.

"But what that demonstrates is absolutely that the French are being effective in preventing a number of these small boats."

"Clearly, every single day that one slips through the net and crosses, it's one too many, and that's why it's absolutely critical to us to not take our foot off the gas and to keep working hard with our French partners and stop this from happening."

In the last week, 425 migrants made it across the Channel on five boats during three days of good weather.

Stopping the trade in equipment for Channel crossings is the first layer of tactics being used by the UK and other countries.

Dinghies, outboard engines, and life preservers have been seized by police in Germany.

Nearer the coast, boats have been discovered buried on beaches and in cars heading for the coast.

With less equipment available, people smugglers have resorted to using bigger boats.

Earlier this month a "mega-dinghy", with 230 people on board , was intercepted in the Channel.

The second layer is to stop migrants launching from beaches.

In July last year a BBC team witnessed the police slashing an inflatable boat with a knife to prevent it being used. This technique is now being used more often.

Interception at sea is the most difficult challenge. The UK government knows if it can prevent migrant boats getting into British waters, where the Border Force is legally obliged to pick them up, the incentive to try to cross will be reduced.

The concern is that smuggling gangs will continue to adapt but Eastaugh told the BBC that changes to their methods demonstrated how hard they are finding it to operate.

"That's why the numbers we're seeing are so successful, and we're absolutely not complacent, and we must keep working this way to keep the numbers down," he said.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "The only way we can stop the crossings is by having a proper deterrent. If people know they can stay in the UK, get put up in a hotel and claim benefits then they will keep risking these dangerous journeys."

Earlier this month Reform UK said if it was in power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.

The French interior ministry responded by saying it would "constitute a violation of French sovereignty".

articles.title: Pakistan’s former leader Imran Khan taken back to prison after hospital check-up
articles.summary: Pakistan’s former leader and cricket icon Imran Khan was taken back to prison Friday morning after a medical check at a private hospital in the capital Islamabad, the government said.
articles.body: Pakistan’s former leader and cricket icon Imran Khan was taken back to prison Friday morning after a medical check at a private hospital in the capital Islamabad, the government said. Khan’s sons told CNN this month they were worried about his health, claiming they were unable to visit him in prison. His family and lawyer had said the ex-prime minister had lost most of his vision in his right eye. Pakistan’s Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on X Friday that Khan was taken to hospital after midnight over a court order and was subsequently returned to Adiala prison following a medical evaluation. “A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist, and a physician, conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit,” the minister said on X. He added that Khan’s sister was present throughout the duration of the examination. The government insists that prisoners are provided with proper medical care and sent to hospital if required. Khan’s transfer to the hospital in the late hours was seen as a win by his supporters and his party, who had long pushed for access to better medical care for Khan. Zulfikar Bukhari, a senior leader from Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaaf (PTI) party had called the move a “constitutional obligation” and not a “political concession.” On Tuesday, Pakistan’s supreme court had ordered Khan to be taken to hospital for a medical examination and necessary treatment, following months of concern over his health. The court had also ordered a medical board to be formed which was to include his personal doctors as well as his sister, Dr Uzma Khan. The court had also reinstated weekly family visits. Khan achieved international fame on the cricket pitch as the formidable captain of Pakistan’s national team, leading the country to its only World Cup victory in 1992. After retirement from the sport, he led the country from 2018 until his ouster in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in 2022. He has been in prison since his conviction a year later on charges of corruption and revealing state secrets which he and his supporters say are a politically motivated response to his opposition to the current government of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

articles.title: Hacker targets ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ in apparent leak
articles.summary: The gaming world has been rattled by what appears to be a major leak of the highly anticipated “Grand Theft Auto VI,” with the alleged hacker warning other publishers that “no one is safe” from similar breaches.
articles.body: The gaming world has been rattled by what appears to be a major leak of the highly anticipated “Grand Theft Auto VI,” with the alleged hacker warning other publishers that “no one is safe” from similar breaches. Rockstar Games, the company behind the blockbuster “GTA” franchise, is known for tightly guarding unreleased material. But this week, multiple gameplay clips and what appears to be the entire “GTA VI” map surfaced online. Rockstar and Take-Two Interactive, its parent company, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Neither has issued a public statement regarding the purported hack. In recent days, multiple social media posts that have shared the apparent leaks have been removed from platforms including X and Reddit. Take Two filed subpoenas petitioning Microsoft and Discord with the Southern District Court of New York on Thursday asking them to release of any records related to the online accounts involved in posting and sharing leaks. Both companies have until Sept. 4 to provide the records, according to the petition for a subpoena, which was first reported by the gaming outlet Kotaku. The hacker, an individual or group calling itself Cyberleek, framed the security breach as a protest against the gaming industry’s shift toward all-digital releases, a trend that has sparked backlash among players. “Publishers sell licenses and call them purchases. They ship unfinished games and call them living services. They lock content on discs and call it DLC,” Cyberleek wrote in a public post on Thursday. “They kill games and keep the money. Every year anti-consumerism tightens its grip, and every year gamers get less for what they pay.” The extremely popular “GTA” franchise — which launched in 1997 — is an action-adventure video game series that follows players driving around fictional cities to complete missions. But for the first time in the franchise’s 28-year history, Rockstar said the newest “GTA” installment will launch without a physical disc. “GTA VI” is officially slated for release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on Nov. 19. Cyberleek’s footage began circulating online just a week before Netflix is set to preview an extended look at the game. The first trailer for the game was released in December 2023. Fans have remained eager for the return of the franchise, which hasn’t had a new installment since “GTA V” in 2013. The Cyberleek incident has stirred mixed reactions among gamers. Some expressed sympathy for the developers, noting that they “deserve to have their work revealed the way Rockstar intended.” Others unleashed their frustrations against Rockstar, arguing that the company “deserved” the leaks. Take-Two Interactive’s stock plummeted on Wednesday amid the chaos. Critics of the purported hacker noted that Cyberleek’s website polls visitors on what leak they want released next and asks them to vote by sending “donations” via crypto. Its latest leaked video called on viewers to “Show support, buy $Cyberleek.” Cyberleek claims donations are meant to fundraise for a “secret project,” the specifics of which “cannot be revealed yet.” “Let it be absolutely clear: this is not a cash grab,” the hacker stated. But Stop Killing Games, a coalition pushing for legal protections to preserve video games, has urged the community to “not send these people your money, no matter how much sympathy you may feel for their actions.” “Using illegal means to make a point is unacceptable to us and does nothing to protect our right to keep using what we paid for,” the group said in a statement on X. “No matter how strongly you disagree with the decisions of upper management at these companies, there are still thousands of developers who worked hard on this project — and they’re the ones being hit the hardest.”

articles.title: Neutrogena addresses backlash over its past brand deal with Hayden Panettiere
articles.summary: Panettiere said this year that the company had severed ties with her over a “morals clause” after she spoke about her postpartum depression.
articles.body: Neutrogena responded Thursday to mounting backlash over its alleged treatment of its former ambassador Hayden Panettiere, saying on Instagram that the company understands it “made her feel unsupported during a very difficult time.” Panettiere, 36, was found unresponsive Sunday at an apartment complex in South Carolina and was pronounced dead at the scene. The coroner’s office said Panettiere’s cause of death is pending further investigation. An autopsy was completed on Monday. After her sudden death, fans began to resurface a podcast interview with the star from earlier this year in which she claimed that Neutrogena, which she described as “a huge part” of her life, severed ties with her over a “morals clause” when she spoke about her experiences with postpartum depression (PPD). Neutrogena’s social media posts were flooded with negative comments toward the brand, with some calling for a boycott. Across TikTok, many people also shared videos describing the beauty brand’s reported treatment of Panettiere as disappointing. Panettiere and her ex-fiancé Wladimir Klitschko welcomed a daughter, Kaya Evdokia Klitschko, in 2014. Four years later, Panettiere gave full custody of Kaya to Klitschko amid what she described to parenting outlet Momé as a “really challenging time in my life.” Panettiere worked with Neutrogena from 2005 to 2015. In its post on Instagram on Thursday, the brand described Panettiere as “a valued member of our Neutrogena community” for more than a decade. “We are proud to have partnered with her and understand that we made her feel unsupported during a very difficult time,” the brand wrote. “This is not what Neutrogena stands for or who we want to be.” The beauty company did not elaborate on the terms of Panettiere’s contract. A spokesperson for the brand did not respond to NBC News’ request for further comment. During her appearance on Jay Shetty’s “On Purpose Podcast” in May, Panettiere told the host that she “had no intention or plan to talk about postpartum depression” but that “it just came up and I was just being honest and never for a second did I think that anyone cared or that anyone would have a bad reaction to it.” She said she thought “this is the last thing that I thought they would ever fire me over.” She continued, “And so when I got that call that Neutrogena wanted to fire me over that, and my representative at the time said, ‘That’s illegal you can’t do that,’ I knew that that was gonna be it, that I was not gonna be invited back the next year, and I had worked with those people for 10 years.” In her memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” which was published in May, Panettiere also elaborated on her struggles with PPD. “Ever since Kaya’s birth, all my natural optimism and pep had vanished,” she wrote. “The three months I planned to take off seemed like an eternity, with long days of nothingness stretching before me. When Kaya cried, I struggled to soothe her, feeling desperate, inadequate, and out of control.” She said she began self-medicating with wine. And in an art-reflecting-life moment, her private struggles drove the drama in Season 4 of “Nashville.” PPD affects 1 in 7 women, according to the Cleveland Clinic. More severe than just the “baby blues,” postpartum depression can be characterized by extreme sadness, anger, trouble bonding with the baby, insomnia or violent ideations. Neutrogena said in the Instagram post that it held off on issuing a statement after Panettiere’s death until now “out of respect for Hayden’s family and loved ones.” “Everyone at Neutrogena extends their deepest condolences to Hayden’s family and all who loved her.” The company said that Panettiere’s “courage in sharing her challenges helped inspire important conversations and awareness.” It pledged to make “a significant investment to a long-standing community health partner to help give more women access to the support they need, including care for postpartum depression.”
